extracted.intended_audience: prospective writers and students (adult and youth) considering Hugo House Summer 2022 classes
extracted.subtask_description: A community-center course catalog listing Summer 2022 creative-writing classes (fiction, nonfiction, poetry, mixed-genre, youth), with course-level learning goals, expectations, and administrative policies for instructors and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: TIERED class level guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: TIERED | These courses are designed to equip you with tools, skills, and an understanding of the diverse voices at work in each genre. You may self-select into classes based on where you feel comfortable. Take these classes as many times as you like.

rubrics_metrics.name: ALL LEVELS class designation
rubrics_metrics.description: ALL LEVELS | Many classes at Hugo House are intended for writers at any level, regardless of prior writing class experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: INTRODUCTORY class designation
rubrics_metrics.description: INTRODUCTORY | Writers with limited experience in a writing class or workshop setting who want to expand their knowledge should consider introductory classes. These classes are also designed for writers who want to explore a new genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: INTERMEDIATE class designation
rubrics_metrics.description: INTERMEDIATE | Writers with some experience in genre-specific instruction looking to deepen their understanding should consider intermediate classes. These classes often feature a workshop component in which student work is shared and critiqued.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADVANCED class designation
rubrics_metrics.description: ADVANCED | Writers with significant experience in a writing class or workshop setting who seek assistance and feedback with revision should consider advanced classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student Guidelines (respect & classroom conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: At all times, please: remain respectful of all writers (and their work) in the classroom; be aware of privilege and how it can affect other students; be intentional in working against traditional power dynamics; be aware that fellow students have an equal right to the class space and time; put aside personal technology if not being used for the purpose of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you experience or witness harassment or discrimination in a Hugo House class, alert the registrar at registrar@hugohouse.org or 206.322.7030. Full Student Guidelines available at hugohouse.org/about/student-guidelines/.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access needs procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: For students with access needs, Hugo House is ready to help. Teachers should reach out about access needs, but please also feel free to notify the registrar of your individual needs before your class begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalog key: asynchronous classes
rubrics_metrics.description: This denotes an asynchronous class. These classes can be done at your own pace throughout the week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund & cancellation policy (schedule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you need to cancel your registration for a class, the following refund schedule applies: 3 days or more before a class, a class credit or transfer will be issued less a 5% fee. Refunds will be issued less a 10% fee. Less than 3 business days before a class starts, no refund, credits, or transfers are available. No refunds, credits, or transfers are available after classes begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Hugo House cancels a class, you will receive a full refund.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordings policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Hugo House does not record classes for students who are absent except in special cases such as religious holidays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration logistics & timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Register by phone or online. All registration opens at 10:30 am PT. Scholarship Donation Day, Member registration, General registration, and Early bird pricing windows and dates are published (e.g., Scholarship Donation Day: May 23; Member registration: May 24; General registration: May 31; Early bird pricing in effect May 23–June 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarship Donation Day: make a $250 (or more) tax-deductible donation to register before registration opens; donations must be made over the phone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarship availability & deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Need-based scholarships are available every quarter. Applications are due May 30, and scholarship applicants will be notified June 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visit hugohouse.org/scholarships for more information and to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: COVID contingency for in-person classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A handful of our summer classes are scheduled to take place in person. Should COVID-19 risks escalate and prohibit teachers or front desk staff from attending in person, these classes may be moved to Zoom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All in-person classes are listed in a separate area of the catalog. For on-site COVID-19 protocols, visit hugohouse.org/about/health-safety-guidelines/.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership benefits & discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hugo House members receive early registration (one week before the general public), discounts on classes and events, discounted tickets, bookstore discounts, audiobook discounts, and a tax-deductible membership value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership details at hugohouse.org/support/become-member/.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript consulting and editorial services
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect with manuscript consultants—all experienced teachers and writers—to receive one-on-one guidance for works-in-progress; applying for awards, residencies, or MFA programs; submitting to agents, magazines, or publishers; or other writerly concerns. Select consultants are also available for line- and copyediting services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See full list of consultants and services at hugohouse.org/about/coaching-mentorship/.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop model: sharing and critique expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many classes include a workshop component in which student work is shared and critiqued; students will give and receive feedback on peers' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'will have the opportunity to develop a story or novel excerpt with peer feedback'; 'Students will be asked to share and read each other's stories ahead of class.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation expectations (readings & pre-class work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes require reading and preparatory work outside of class, including reading published work, preparing drafts to share, and reading peers' submissions ahead of class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in catalog: 'We will read and discuss published work'; 'Students will be asked to share and read each other's stories ahead of class.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative in-class practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Many courses use in-class generative writing exercises and prompts designed to produce new drafts and practice techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course texts repeatedly state: 'be prepared to write (and draw, etc.)', 'in-class, guided writing prompts', and 'will engage in in-class writing, sharing our work, and a discussion...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Output expectations (page/draft targets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes specify production goals (e.g., Creative Nonfiction I: 'Students will generate 15-20 pages' ; Poetry courses: 'Students will generate four to six new poems').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should expect to produce specified amounts of work during the course and submit drafts for workshop as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission-to-publication practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses like 'Poetry & Publishing' require students to submit to a literary journal for publication and to finish class by sending at least one submission including a new, strong cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Students will generate four to six new poems, participate in a mock editorial committee, and submit work to a literary journal for publication.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene construction blueprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Blueprint for constructing scenes: learn to make a visual blueprint that organizes and cements critical elements of scenes, including measured actions, plotted conflicts, artistic hooks, and evocative settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on structural scene elements and foundations so scenes are not 'shaky'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time as a tool for tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Time management in fiction: the story timeline and the reader's patience must interact to keep tension taut; practice careful management of time to increase tension and power in fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to authors (Joy Williams, Colson Whitehead, Chekhov) for guidance and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development (including static/depthful characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing characters of depth, including those whose circumstances leave them little room for change; explore how plot events, atmosphere, setting, and internal fears shape characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reading, discussion, writing exercises, and workshop feedback to refine character portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Write natural conversations that advance the plot and give insight into characters; practice through small group exercises and analysis of excerpts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course notes: 'Dialogue makes up between 30% and 70% of the average novel—it's a deceptively tricky art to master.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision-focused techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Short story revision workshop: isolate and revise different elements each week (plot, setting, character, language) using cutting, highlighting, discussion, and iterative pushing of the same piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be prepared to share and read peers' stories ahead of class and bring a single piece to focus revision across sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding: exterior and interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilding 'Outside & In' covers building exterior worlds (place, culture, atmosphere) and interior worlds (needs, wants, fears, repressed desires, wounds) and how interior history shows up in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class includes early weeks on exterior, middle weeks on interior, and a final week focused on workshopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical fiction research & imaginative reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach research, world-building, and character development in historical fiction, with specific focus on reimagining spaces and voices not well-documented in the historical record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course includes guided writing exercises and class discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash nonfiction craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-form nonfiction: read and analyze flash nonfiction pieces under ~750 words; learn tenets of the form and engage in writing and revising exercises to create impactful short work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes concise power and revision strategies for tight forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric essay techniques and risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with lyric essays using constraints, fragments, flash forms; explore meaning stitched through association, imagery, and pathways of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read authors (Hanif Abdurraqib, Natalie Diaz, Melissa Febos) and engage with generative exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food writing: craft, pitching, and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop drafts, craft publication pitches, find appropriate editors, and discuss politics and ethics of food writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss contemporary food writers and learn to position work for publication; includes practical pitch exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short essays for online publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clear, compelling short essays (750–1,000 words) for internet publications: identify themes, outline, craft calls to action, and tailor writing to target publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice pitches and receive assignment-style homework to build publication-ready pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry craft fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry I emphasizes image, metaphor, sound, lineation, and structure; introduces the workshop model for reading and writing poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students will write and submit poems for peer and instructor feedback; goals include familiarity with poetic devices and drafting new poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry & publishing (practical submission skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate poems, participate in a mock editorial committee, become familiar with literary journals, and submit at least one poem with a strong cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read contemporary poets and finish course by sending a submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found text strategies in poetry (erasure & collage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore strategies for 'haunting' poems via erasure (removing portions while maintaining sequence) and collage (interweaving found text with original poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sample poems as models and compose original pieces incorporating found text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative memoir & genre hybridization
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative memoir blends personal identity, lived experience, and imaginative impulse, inviting fictional elements that enhance and contradict truth; includes in-class writing, sharing, and discussion about memoir/fiction challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages rule-breaking and risk in merging genres while examining craft implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing across cultures: responsible portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine strategies for researching and portraying lives unlike our own that reflect social and historical context and the fullness of a character's humanity; discuss cultural appropriation and responsible, respectful cross-identity writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on writing exercises and discuss texts by authors who model responsible cross-cultural writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing politics, history, and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss issues common to story-writing—plotting, pacing, imagery, rhythm—through close readings and address how to deal with history, politics, problems of representation, and translation for minority writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close reading of specific texts as case studies (e.g., Carolyn Forché's 'The Colonel').

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor writing & punch-up methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for finding and translating humor onto the page, including 'writers' room' punch-up sessions for essays, stories, monologues, and screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring existing pieces to share and collaboratively 'punch up' comedic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: From page to stage (performance adaptation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft personal experience into a compelling story, then adapt words for spoken performance; examine differences between written and spoken word and add performance elements to engage audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part workshop with writing then performance practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming perfectionism & producing drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Get past perfectionism and procrastination using prompts to produce draft material quickly; embrace 'shitty first drafts' to generate work for later revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes quantity and momentum as tools against creative blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production bootstraps: finishing and re-invigoration strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: For writers struggling with books: examine when to revise vs. continue drafting; ask productive vs. counterproductive questions; seek ways to re-invigorate sustained writing toward finishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered asynchronously via Wet Ink; sessions done at one's own pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation & readiness (be prepared to share & listen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many class descriptions explicitly state students should 'be prepared to write... and please be prepared to share and listen'—indicating an expectation of active participation, sharing drafts, and listening to peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies across generative workshops, in-class exercises, and critique sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youth program structure & commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth offerings include weekly write-ins, camps, and the Young Writers Cohort; Cohort applicants devote 80+ hours over eight months to workshopping, studying literature, submitting work, attending events, and supporting youth initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohort application dates and program commitments are specified (e.g., opens Aug. 12; closes Sep. 12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sliding scale & Pay What You Can options
rubrics_metrics.description: Some camps and classes operate on a sliding scale; certain workshops are offered 'Pay What You Can' to increase accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarships and sliding rates are available; camps remain on a sliding scale with scholarship assistance provided as needed.
